   648	### Forced Pod termination {#pod-termination-forced}
   649	
   650	{{< caution >}}
   651	Forced deletions can be potentially disruptive for some workloads and their Pods.
   652	{{< /caution >}}
   653	
   654	By default, all deletes are graceful within 30 seconds. The `kubectl delete` command supports
   655	the `--grace-period=<seconds>` option which allows you to override the default and specify your
   656	own value.
   657	
   658	Setting the grace period to `0` forcibly and immediately deletes the Pod from the API
   659	server. If the Pod was still running on a node, that forcible deletion triggers the kubelet to
   660	begin immediate cleanup.
   661	
   662	Using kubectl, You must specify an additional flag `--force` along with `--grace-period=0`
   663	in order to perform force deletions.
   664	
   665	When a force deletion is performed, the API server does not wait for confirmation
   666	from the kubelet that the Pod has been terminated on the node it was running on. It
   667	removes the Pod in the API immediately so a new Pod can be created with the same
   668	name. On the node, Pods that are set to terminate immediately will still be given
   669	a small grace period before being force killed.
   670	
   671	{{< caution >}}
   672	Immediate deletion does not wait for confirmation that the running resource has been terminated.
   673	The resource may continue to run on the cluster indefinitely.
   674	{{< /caution >}}
   675	
   676	If you need to force-delete Pods that are part of a StatefulSet, refer to the task
   677	documentation for
   678	[deleting Pods from a StatefulSet](/docs/tasks/run-application/force-delete-stateful-set-pod/).
   679	
   680	### Pod shutdown and sidecar containers {##termination-with-sidecars}
   681	
   682	If your Pod includes one or more
   683	[sidecar containers](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/sidecar-containers/)
   684	(init containers with an Always restart policy), the kubelet will delay sending
   685	the TERM signal to these sidecar containers until the last main container has fully terminated.
   686	The sidecar containers will be terminated in the reverse order they are defined in the Pod spec.
   687	This ensures that sidecar containers continue serving the other containers in the Pod until they
   688	are no longer needed.
   689	
   690	This means that slow termination of a main container will also delay the termination of the sidecar containers.
   691	If the grace period expires before the termination process is complete, the Pod may enter [forced termination](#pod-termination-beyond-grace-period).
   692	In this case, all remaining containers in the Pod will be terminated simultaneously with a short grace period.
   693	
   694	Similarly, if the Pod has a `preStop` hook that exceeds the termination grace period, emergency termination may occur.
   695	In general, if you have used `preStop` hooks to control the termination order without sidecar containers, you can now
   696	remove them and allow the kubelet to manage sidecar termination automatically.
   697	
   698	### Garbage collection of Pods {#pod-garbage-collection}
   699	
   700	For failed Pods, the API objects remain in the cluster's API until a human or
   701	{{< glossary_tooltip term_id="controller" text="controller" >}} process
   702	explicitly removes them.
   703	
   704	The Pod garbage collector (PodGC), which is a controller in the control plane, cleans up
   705	terminated Pods (with a phase of `Succeeded` or `Failed`), when the number of Pods exceeds the
   706	configured threshold (determined by `terminated-pod-gc-threshold` in the kube-controller-manager).
   707	This avoids a resource leak as Pods are created and terminated over time.
   708	
   709	Additionally, PodGC cleans up any Pods which satisfy any of the following conditions:
   710	
   711	1. are orphan Pods - bound to a node which no longer exists,
   712	1. are unscheduled terminating Pods,
   713	1. are terminating Pods, bound to a non-ready node tainted with
   714	   [`node.kubernetes.io/out-of-service`](/docs/reference/labels-annotations-taints/#node-kubernetes-io-out-of-service).

    74	Figure 1. HorizontalPodAutoscaler controls the scale of a Deployment and its ReplicaSet
    75	
    76	Kubernetes implements horizontal pod autoscaling as a control loop that runs intermittently
    77	(it is not a continuous process). The interval is set by the
    78	`--horizontal-pod-autoscaler-sync-period` parameter to the
    79	[`kube-controller-manager`](/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/kube-controller-manager/)
    80	(and the default interval is 15 seconds).
    81	
    82	Once during each period, the controller manager queries the resource utilization against the
    83	metrics specified in each HorizontalPodAutoscaler definition. The controller manager
    84	finds the target resource defined by the `scaleTargetRef`,
    85	then selects the pods based on the target resource's `.spec.selector` labels,
    86	and obtains the metrics from either the resource metrics API (for per-pod resource metrics),
    87	or the custom metrics API (for all other metrics).
    88	
    89	- For per-pod resource metrics (like CPU), the controller fetches the metrics
    90	  from the resource metrics API for each Pod targeted by the HorizontalPodAutoscaler.
    91	  Then, if a target utilization value is set, the controller calculates the utilization
    92	  value as a percentage of the equivalent
    93	  [resource request](/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers/#requests-and-limits)
    94	  on the containers in each Pod. If a target raw value is set, the raw metric values are used directly.
    95	  The controller then takes the mean of the utilization or the raw value (depending on the type
    96	  of target specified) across all targeted Pods, and produces a ratio used to scale
    97	  the number of desired replicas.
    98	
    99	  Please note that if some of the Pod's containers do not have the relevant resource request set,
   100	  CPU utilization for the Pod will not be defined and the autoscaler will
   101	  not take any action for that metric. See the [algorithm details](#algorithm-details) section below
   102	  for more information about how the autoscaling algorithm works.
   103	
   104	- For per-pod custom metrics, the controller functions similarly to per-pod resource metrics,
   105	  except that it works with raw values, not utilization values.
   106	
   107	- For object metrics and external metrics, a single metric is fetched, which describes
   108	  the object in question. This metric is compared to the target
   109	  value, to produce a ratio as above. In the `autoscaling/v2` API
   110	  version, this value can optionally be divided by the number of Pods before the
   111	  comparison is made.
   112	
   113	The common use for HorizontalPodAutoscaler is to configure it to fetch metrics from
   114	{{< glossary_tooltip text="aggregated APIs" term_id="aggregation-layer" >}}
   115	(`metrics.k8s.io`, `custom.metrics.k8s.io`, or `external.metrics.k8s.io`). The `metrics.k8s.io` API is
   116	usually provided by an add-on named Metrics Server, which needs to be launched separately.
   117	For more information about resource metrics, see
   118	[Metrics Server](/docs/tasks/debug/debug-cluster/resource-metrics-pipeline/#metrics-server).
   119	
   120	[Support for metrics APIs](#support-for-metrics-apis) explains the stability guarantees and support status for these
   121	different APIs.
   122	
   123	The HorizontalPodAutoscaler controller accesses corresponding workload resources that support scaling (such as Deployments
   124	and StatefulSet). These resources each have a subresource named `scale`, an interface that allows you to dynamically set the
   125	number of replicas and examine each of their current states.
   126	For general information about subresources in the Kubernetes API, see
   127	[Kubernetes API Concepts](/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/).
   128	
   129	### Algorithm details
   130	
   131	From the most basic perspective, the HorizontalPodAutoscaler controller
   132	operates on the ratio between desired metric value and current metric
   133	value:
   134	
   135	```math
   136	\begin{equation*}
   137	desiredReplicas = ceil\left\lceil currentReplicas \times \frac{currentMetricValue}{desiredMetricValue} \right\rceil
   138	\end{equation*}
   139	```
   140	
   141	For example, if the current metric value is `200m`, and the desired value
   142	is `100m`, the number of replicas will be doubled, since
   143	\\( { 200.0 \div 100.0 } = 2.0 \\).  
   144	If the current value is instead `50m`, you'll halve the number of
   145	replicas, since \\( { 50.0 \div 100.0 } = 0.5 \\). The control plane skips any scaling
   146	action if the ratio is sufficiently close to 1.0 (within a globally-configurable
   147	tolerance, 0.1 by default).
   148	
   149	When a `targetAverageValue` or `targetAverageUtilization` is specified,
   150	the `currentMetricValue` is computed by taking the average of the given
   151	metric across all Pods in the HorizontalPodAutoscaler's scale target.
   152	
   153	Before checking the tolerance and deciding on the final values, the control
   154	plane also considers whether any metrics are missing, and how many Pods
   155	are [`Ready`](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#pod-conditions).

   157	in the process of being shut down / removed) are ignored, and all failed Pods
   158	are discarded.
   159	
   160	If a particular Pod is missing metrics, it is set aside for later; Pods
   161	with missing metrics will be used to adjust the final scaling amount.
   162	
   163	When scaling on CPU, if any pod has yet to become ready (it's still
   164	initializing, or possibly is unhealthy) _or_ the most recent metric point for
   165	the pod was before it became ready, that pod is set aside as well.

   167	Due to technical constraints, the HorizontalPodAutoscaler controller
   168	cannot exactly determine the first time a pod becomes ready when

   170	considers a Pod "not yet ready" if it's unready and transitioned to
   171	ready within a short, configurable window of time since it started.
   172	This value is configured with the `--horizontal-pod-autoscaler-initial-readiness-delay`
   173	flag, and its default is 30 seconds.
   174	Once a pod has become ready, it considers any transition to

   176	since it started. This value is configured with the
   177	`--horizontal-pod-autoscaler-cpu-initialization-period` flag, and its
   178	default is 5 minutes.

   186	the magnitude of any potential scale.
   187

   190	the controller conservatively assumes that the not-yet-ready pods are consuming 0%
   191	of the desired metric, further dampening the magnitude of a scale up.
   192	
   193	After factoring in the not-yet-ready pods and missing metrics, the
   194	controller recalculates the usage ratio. If the new ratio reverses the scale

   203	
   204	If multiple metrics are specified in a HorizontalPodAutoscaler, this

    47	Network policies are implemented by the [network plugin](/docs/concepts/extend-kubernetes/compute-storage-net/network-plugins/).
    48	To use network policies, you must be using a networking solution which supports NetworkPolicy.
    49	Creating a NetworkPolicy resource without a controller that implements it will have no effect.

    51	## The two sorts of pod isolation
    52	
    53	There are two sorts of isolation for a pod: isolation for egress, and isolation for ingress.
    54	They concern what connections may be established. "Isolation" here is not absolute, rather it
    55	means "some restrictions apply". The alternative, "non-isolated for $direction", means that no
    56	restrictions apply in the stated direction. The two sorts of isolation (or not) are declared
    57	independently, and are both relevant for a connection from one pod to another.
    58	
    59	By default, a pod is non-isolated for egress; all outbound connections are allowed.
    60	A pod is isolated for egress if there is any NetworkPolicy that both selects the pod and has
    61	"Egress" in its `policyTypes`; we say that such a policy applies to the pod for egress.
    62	When a pod is isolated for egress, the only allowed connections from the pod are those allowed by
    63	the `egress` list of some NetworkPolicy that applies to the pod for egress. Reply traffic for those
    64	allowed connections will also be implicitly allowed.
    65	The effects of those `egress` lists combine additively.
    66	
    67	By default, a pod is non-isolated for ingress; all inbound connections are allowed.
    68	A pod is isolated for ingress if there is any NetworkPolicy that both selects the pod and
    69	has "Ingress" in its `policyTypes`; we say that such a policy applies to the pod for ingress.
    70	When a pod is isolated for ingress, the only allowed connections into the pod are those from
    71	the pod's node and those allowed by the `ingress` list of some NetworkPolicy that applies to
    72	the pod for ingress. Reply traffic for those allowed connections will also be implicitly allowed.
    73	The effects of those `ingress` lists combine additively.
    74	
    75	Network policies do not conflict; they are additive. If any policy or policies apply to a given
    76	pod for a given direction, the connections allowed in that direction from that pod is the union of
    77	what the applicable policies allow. Thus, order of evaluation does not affect the policy result.
    78	
    79	For a connection from a source pod to a destination pod to be allowed, both the egress policy on
    80	the source pod and the ingress policy on the destination pod need to allow the connection. If
    81	either side does not allow the connection, it will not happen.

    27	## Requests and limits
    28	
    29	If the node where a Pod is running has enough of a resource available, it's possible (and
    30	allowed) for a container to use more resource than its `request` for that resource specifies.
    31	
    32	For example, if you set a `memory` request of 256 MiB for a container, and that container is in
    33	a Pod scheduled to a Node with 8GiB of memory and no other Pods, then the container can try to use
    34	more RAM.
    35	
    36	Limits are a different story. Both `cpu` and `memory` limits are applied by the kubelet (and
    37	{{< glossary_tooltip text="container runtime" term_id="container-runtime" >}}),
    38	and are ultimately enforced by the kernel. On Linux nodes, the Linux kernel
    39	enforces limits with
    40	{{< glossary_tooltip text="cgroups" term_id="cgroup" >}}.
    41	The behavior of `cpu` and `memory` limit enforcement is slightly different.
    42	
    43	`cpu` limits are enforced by CPU throttling. When a container approaches
    44	its `cpu` limit, the kernel will restrict access to the CPU corresponding to the
    45	container's limit. Thus, a `cpu` limit is a hard limit the kernel enforces.
    46	Containers may not use more CPU than is specified in their `cpu` limit.
    47	
    48	`memory` limits are enforced by the kernel with out of memory (OOM) kills. When
    49	a container uses more than its `memory` limit, the kernel may terminate it. However,
    50	terminations only happen when the kernel detects memory pressure. Thus, a
    51	container that over allocates memory may not be immediately killed. This means
    52	`memory` limits are enforced reactively. A container may use more memory than
    53	its `memory` limit, but if it does, it may get killed.
    54	
    55	{{< note >}}
    56	There is an alpha feature `MemoryQoS` which attempts to add more preemptive
    57	limit enforcement for memory (as opposed to reactive enforcement by the OOM
    58	killer). However, this effort is
    59	[stalled](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/a47155b340/keps/sig-node/2570-memory-qos#latest-update-stalled)
    60	due to a potential livelock situation a memory hungry can cause.
    61	{{< /note >}}
    62	
    63	{{< note >}}
    64	If you specify a limit for a resource, but do not specify any request, and no admission-time
    65	mechanism has applied a default request for that resource, then Kubernetes copies the limit
    66	you specified and uses it as the requested value for the resource.
    67	{{< /note >}}
    68	
    69	## Resource types
    70	
    71	*CPU* and *memory* are each a *resource type*. A resource type has a base unit.
    72	CPU represents compute processing and is specified in units of [Kubernetes CPUs](#meaning-of-cpu).
    73	Memory is specified in units of bytes.
    74	For Linux workloads, you can specify _huge page_ resources.
    75	Huge pages are a Linux-specific feature where the node kernel allocates blocks of memory
    76	that are much larger than the default page size.
    77	
    78	For example, on a system where the default page size is 4KiB, you could specify a limit,
    79	`hugepages-2Mi: 80Mi`. If the container tries allocating over 40 2MiB huge pages (a
    80	total of 80 MiB), that allocation fails.
    81	
    82	{{< note >}}
    83	You cannot overcommit `hugepages-*` resources.
    84	This is different from the `memory` and `cpu` resources.
    85	{{< /note >}}

    87	CPU and memory are collectively referred to as *compute resources*, or *resources*. Compute
    88	resources are measurable quantities that can be requested, allocated, and
    89	consumed. They are distinct from

    91	[Services](/docs/concepts/services-networking/service/) are objects that can be read and modified

   410	  `whenScaled` policy, only PVCs corresponding to Pod replicas being scaled down are
   411	  deleted, after their Pods have been deleted.
   412	
   413	`Retain` (default)
   414	: PVCs from the `volumeClaimTemplate` are not affected when their Pod is
   415	  deleted. This is the behavior before this new feature.
   416	
   417	Bear in mind that these policies **only** apply when Pods are being removed due to the
   418	StatefulSet being deleted or scaled down. For example, if a Pod associated with a StatefulSet
   419	fails due to node failure, and the control plane creates a replacement Pod, the StatefulSet
   420	retains the existing PVC.  The existing volume is unaffected, and the cluster will attach it to
   421	the node where the new Pod is about to launch.
   422	  
   423	The default for policies is `Retain`, matching the StatefulSet behavior before this new feature.
   424	
   425	Here is an example policy.
   426	
   427	```yaml
   428	apiVersion: apps/v1
   429	kind: StatefulSet
   430	...
   431	spec:
   432	  persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy:
   433	    whenDeleted: Retain
   434	    whenScaled: Delete
   435	...
   436	```

   438	The StatefulSet {{<glossary_tooltip text="controller" term_id="controller">}} adds
   439	[owner references](/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/owners-dependents/#owner-references-in-object-specifications)
   440	to its PVCs, which are then deleted by the {{<glossary_tooltip text="garbage collector"
   441	term_id="garbage-collection">}} after the Pod is terminated. This enables the Pod to
   442	cleanly unmount all volumes before the PVCs are deleted (and before the backing PV and
   443	volume are deleted, depending on the retain policy).  When you set the `whenDeleted`
   444	policy to `Delete`, an owner reference to the StatefulSet instance is placed on all PVCs
   445	associated with that StatefulSet.
   446	
   447	The `whenScaled` policy must delete PVCs only when a Pod is scaled down, and not when a
   448	Pod is deleted for another reason. When reconciling, the StatefulSet controller compares
   449	its desired replica count to the actual Pods present on the cluster. Any StatefulSet Pod
   450	whose id greater than the replica count is condemned and marked for deletion. If the
   451	`whenScaled` policy is `Delete`, the condemned Pods are first set as owners to the
   452	associated StatefulSet template PVCs, before the Pod is deleted. This causes the PVCs
   453	to be garbage collected after only the condemned Pods have terminated.
   454	
   455	This means that if the controller crashes and restarts, no Pod will be deleted before its
   456	owner reference has been updated appropriate to the policy. If a condemned Pod is
   457	force-deleted while the controller is down, the owner reference may or may not have been
   458	set up, depending on when the controller crashed. It may take several reconcile loops to
   459	update the owner references, so some condemned Pods may have set up owner references and
   460	others may not. For this reason we recommend waiting for the controller to come back up,
   461	which will verify owner references before terminating Pods. If that is not possible, the

   298	### Node Isolation
   299	
   300	Node isolation is another technique that you can use to isolate tenant workloads from each other.
   301	With node isolation, a set of nodes is dedicated to running pods from a particular tenant and

   303	all pods running on a node will belong to a single tenant. The risk of information disclosure is
   304	slightly lower with node isolation because an attacker that manages to escape from a container
   305	will only have access to the containers and volumes mounted to that node.

   308	aware that the kubelet and (unless using virtual control planes) the API service are still shared
   309	services. A skilled attacker could use the permissions assigned to the kubelet or other pods
   310	running on the node to move laterally within the cluster and gain access to tenant workloads
   311	running on other nodes. If this is a major concern, consider implementing compensating controls
   312	such as seccomp, AppArmor or SELinux or explore using sandboxed containers or creating separate
   313	clusters for each tenant.

   316	containers since you can charge back per node rather than per pod. It also has fewer compatibility
   317	and performance issues and may be easier to implement than sandboxing containers.

   607	## Immutable Secrets {#secret-immutable}

   609	{{< feature-state for_k8s_version="v1.21" state="stable" >}}
   610	
   611	Kubernetes lets you mark specific Secrets (and ConfigMaps) as _immutable_.
   612	Preventing changes to the data of an existing Secret has the following benefits:
   613	
   614	- protects you from accidental (or unwanted) updates that could cause applications outages
   615	- (for clusters that extensively use Secrets - at least tens of thousands of unique Secret
   616	  to Pod mounts), switching to immutable Secrets improves the performance of your cluster
   617	  by significantly reducing load on kube-apiserver. The kubelet does not need to maintain
   618	  a [watch] on any Secrets that are marked as immutable.
   619	
   620	### Marking a Secret as immutable {#secret-immutable-create}
   621	
   622	You can create an immutable Secret by setting the `immutable` field to `true`. For example,
   623	
   624	```yaml
   625	apiVersion: v1
   626	kind: Secret
   627	metadata: ...
   628	data: ...
   629	immutable: true
   630	```
   631	
   632	You can also update any existing mutable Secret to make it immutable.
   633	
   634	{{< note >}}
   635	Once a Secret or ConfigMap is marked as immutable, it is _not_ possible to revert this change
   636	nor to mutate the contents of the `data` field. You can only delete and recreate the Secret.
   637	Existing Pods maintain a mount point to the deleted Secret - it is recommended to recreate
   638	these pods.

   641	## Information security for Secrets
   642	
   643	Although ConfigMap and Secret work similarly, Kubernetes applies some additional
   644	protection for Secret objects.
   645	
   646	Secrets often hold values that span a spectrum of importance, many of which can
   647	cause escalations within Kubernetes (e.g. service account tokens) and to
   648	external systems. Even if an individual app can reason about the power of the
   649	Secrets it expects to interact with, other apps within the same namespace can
   650	render those assumptions invalid.
   651	
   652	A Secret is only sent to a node if a Pod on that node requires it.
   653	For mounting Secrets into Pods, the kubelet stores a copy of the data into a `tmpfs`
   654	so that the confidential data is not written to durable storage.
   655	Once the Pod that depends on the Secret is deleted, the kubelet deletes its local copy
   656	of the confidential data from the Secret.
   657	
   658	There may be several containers in a Pod. By default, containers you define
   659	only have access to the default ServiceAccount and its related Secret.
   660	You must explicitly define environment variables or map a volume into a
   661	container in order to provide access to any other Secret.
   662	
   663	There may be Secrets for several Pods on the same node. However, only the
   664	Secrets that a Pod requests are potentially visible within its containers.
   665	Therefore, one Pod does not have access to the Secrets of another Pod.
   666	
   667	### Configure least-privilege access to Secrets
   668

   172	### Quotas
   173	
   174	Kubernetes workloads consume node resources, like CPU and memory.  In a multi-tenant environment,
   175	you can use [Resource Quotas](/docs/concepts/policy/resource-quotas/) to manage resource usage of
   176	tenant workloads.  For the multiple teams use case, where tenants have access to the Kubernetes
   177	API, you can use resource quotas to limit the number of API resources (for example: the number of
   178	Pods, or the number of ConfigMaps) that a tenant can create. Limits on object count ensure
   179	fairness and aim to avoid _noisy neighbor_ issues from affecting other tenants that share a
   180	control plane.
   181	
   182	Resource quotas are namespaced objects. By mapping tenants to namespaces, cluster admins can use
   183	quotas to ensure that a tenant cannot monopolize a cluster's resources or overwhelm its control
   184	plane. Namespace management tools simplify the administration of quotas. In addition, while
   185	Kubernetes quotas only apply within a single namespace, some namespace management tools allow
   186	groups of namespaces to share quotas, giving administrators far more flexibility with less effort
   187	than built-in quotas.
   188	
   189	Quotas prevent a single tenant from consuming greater than their allocated share of resources
   190	hence minimizing the “noisy neighbor” issue, where one tenant negatively impacts the performance
   191	of other tenants' workloads.
   192	
   193	When you apply a quota to namespace, Kubernetes requires you to also specify resource requests and
   194	limits for each container. Limits are the upper bound for the amount of resources that a container
   195	can consume. Containers that attempt to consume resources that exceed the configured limits will
   196	either be throttled or killed, based on the resource type. When resource requests are set lower
   197	than limits, each container is guaranteed the requested amount but there may still be some
   198	potential for impact across workloads.
   199	
   200	Quotas cannot protect against all kinds of resource sharing, such as network traffic.
   201	Node isolation (described below) may be a better solution for this problem.

   203	## Data Plane Isolation
   204	
   205	Data plane isolation ensures that pods and workloads for different tenants are sufficiently
   206	isolated.
   207	
   208	### Network isolation
   209	
   210	By default, all pods in a Kubernetes cluster are allowed to communicate with each other, and all
   211	network traffic is unencrypted. This can lead to security vulnerabilities where traffic is
   212	accidentally or maliciously sent to an unintended destination, or is intercepted by a workload on
   213	a compromised node.
   214	
   215	Pod-to-pod communication can be controlled using [Network Policies](/docs/concepts/services-networking/network-policies/),
   216	which restrict communication between pods using namespace labels or IP address ranges.
   217	In a multi-tenant environment where strict network isolation between tenants is required, starting
   218	with a default policy that denies communication between pods is recommended with another rule that
   219	allows all pods to query the DNS server for name resolution. With such a default policy in place,
   220	you can begin adding more permissive rules that allow for communication within a namespace.
   221	It is also recommended not to use empty label selector '{}' for namespaceSelector field in network policy definition,
   222	in case traffic need to be allowed between namespaces.
   223	This scheme can be further refined as required. Note that this only applies to pods within a single
   224	control plane; pods that belong to different virtual control planes cannot talk to each other via
   225	Kubernetes networking.
   226	
   227	Namespace management tools may simplify the creation of default or common network policies.
   228	In addition, some of these tools allow you to enforce a consistent set of namespace labels across
   229	your cluster, ensuring that they are a trusted basis for your policies.
   230	
   231	{{< warning >}}
   232	Network policies require a [CNI plugin](/docs/concepts/extend-kubernetes/compute-storage-net/network-plugins/#cni)
   233	that supports the implementation of network policies. Otherwise, NetworkPolicy resources will be ignored.
   234	{{< /warning >}}
   235	
   236	More advanced network isolation may be provided by service meshes, which provide OSI Layer 7
   237	policies based on workload identity, in addition to namespaces. These higher-level policies can
   238	make it easier to manage namespace-based multi-tenancy, especially when multiple namespaces are
   239	dedicated to a single tenant. They frequently also offer encryption using mutual TLS, protecting
   240	your data even in the presence of a compromised node, and work across dedicated or virtual clusters.
   241	However, they can be significantly more complex to manage and may not be appropriate for all users.

   617	  node group) is scaled to zero nodes, and you're expecting the cluster to scale up,
   618	  because, in this case, those topology domains won't be considered until there is

**Decision memo — revise before production approval.** The proposed fields do not establish an end-to-end availability, security, or durability guarantee. Approve only after the configuration changes and validation below. Citations refer exclusively to the supplied Kubernetes v1.32 corpus; recommendations are configuration choices derived from those documented behaviors.

1. **PDB protection depends on the disruption.** Node failure is involuntary: a PDB cannot prevent it, although unavailable Pods count against the budget. During a node drain using the Eviction API, a correctly selected `minAvailable: 5` PDB restricts voluntary eviction; with six healthy replicas, it permits one disruption, and further evictions can block. Direct deletion bypasses this protection. Deployment rolling updates are explicitly unconstrained by PDBs, so `maxUnavailable: 2` permits rollout availability to fall to four. Choose `maxUnavailable: 1`, `maxSurge: 1`, or more conservatively zero unavailable with one surge, and provide scheduling capacity. These control rollout actions, not simultaneous failures. See [disruptions, lines 107–140](/private/tmp/doktimoi-bench-2-competitor-jeIJrI/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/disruptions.md:107) and [Deployment, lines 1183–1211](/private/tmp/doktimoi-bench-2-competitor-jeIJrI/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment.md:1183).

2. **Spread explicitly across zones.** Use an application label selector, `topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone`, and `maxSkew: 1`. The topology key groups equally labelled nodes into domains. With `DoNotSchedule`, skew bounds matching Pods in the target domain relative to the global minimum; unsatisfiable placements remain pending. `ScheduleAnyway` instead prefers reduced skew while allowing imbalance. Recommend hard spreading normally, with an explicit outage policy. When a zone becomes unavailable, placement depends on eligible domains, taints, and capacity: `minDomains: 3` makes the global minimum zero when fewer than three domains remain eligible, potentially blocking replacements. Soft spreading favors placement but sacrifices strict balance. Six balanced replicas imply two per zone, so losing one can leave four. Scheduling constraints do not preserve balance after removals. See [spread definitions, lines 82–130](/private/tmp/doktimoi-bench-2-competitor-jeIJrI/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/topology-spread-constraints.md:82), [eligibility and labels, lines 167–211](/private/tmp/doktimoi-bench-2-competitor-jeIJrI/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/topology-spread-constraints.md:167), and [limitations, lines 605–619](/private/tmp/doktimoi-bench-2-competitor-jeIJrI/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/topology-spread-constraints.md:605).

3. **Separate startup, readiness, and liveness.** Configure a startup probe with sufficient failure threshold and period for measured startup duration. Other probes remain disabled until startup succeeds. Startup failure kills the container, with restart governed by its restart policy; liveness failure similarly triggers killing and restart. Readiness should indicate whether requests can actually succeed, including required database availability where appropriate. Readiness failure removes the Pod from matching Service endpoints without itself restarting the container. Liveness should assess application health independently of a temporary database outage. HTTP health endpoints are suitable if the application implements those meanings; their correctness is an application prerequisite. See [probe behavior, lines 479–497](/private/tmp/doktimoi-bench-2-competitor-jeIJrI/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle.md:479) and [probe selection, lines 512–557](/private/tmp/doktimoi-bench-2-competitor-jeIJrI/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle.md:512).

4. **Thirty seconds is a shutdown budget, not a request-completion guarantee.** Deletion records the grace period before local shutdown begins. The kubelet runs `preStop` first when configured and grace is nonzero, then requests TERM delivery to container process 1. Hook execution consumes the grace period; it does not precede a fresh thirty-second allowance. An overlong hook receives a small, one-off two-second extension. Remaining processes receive SIGKILL when grace expires. Concurrently, terminating endpoints remain temporarily in EndpointSlices with `ready: false`; `serving` supports draining-aware consumers. Size grace for hook work and measured request draining, and implement signal handling. The docs do not establish completion of arbitrary long requests or instantaneous traffic convergence. See [termination, lines 565–639](/private/tmp/doktimoi-bench-2-competitor-jeIJrI/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle.md:565).

5. **Set resource requests deliberately.** CPU requests inform scheduling and provide the denominator for utilization-based HPA; they are not CPU ceilings. Containers can exceed requests when resources permit. CPU limits enforce throttling, potentially affecting latency. Memory limits use reactive OOM killing rather than analogous throttling; excess allocation need not cause immediate termination. Configure measured CPU and memory requests and tested limits. If relevant containers lack effective CPU requests, Pod CPU utilization is undefined and HPA takes no action for that metric. Check admitted values: a limit can become the request when no request or admission default exists. See [resources, lines 18–66](/private/tmp/doktimoi-bench-2-competitor-jeIJrI/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers.md:18) and [HPA utilization, lines 89–102](/private/tmp/doktimoi-bench-2-competitor-jeIJrI/docs/tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md:89).

6. **Expect conservative HPA decisions.** The basic calculation rounds up current replicas multiplied by current-to-target utilization. Missing metrics are initially set aside, then assumed at 100% of target for downscaling and 0% for upscaling. Not-yet-ready CPU Pods are also set aside; during potential upscaling they are conservatively treated as consuming zero. Readiness interpretation uses configurable timing windows, defaulting to thirty seconds and five minutes. Recalculation can cancel scaling if direction reverses or enters tolerance, default 10%. Downscale stabilization selects the highest recommendation within a default five-minute window. Consequently, displayed utilization and the raw ratio need not predict the action. Verify the separately supplied resource metrics API. See [HPA, lines 113–118 and 129–218](/private/tmp/doktimoi-bench-2-competitor-jeIJrI/docs/tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md:113).

7. **Replace default allow with explicit communication permissions.** Select API and database Pods with default-deny ingress and egress policies, then allow approved callers to the API port, API egress to the database port, and corresponding database ingress. Add required DNS access and explicitly inventory other dependencies. Ingress and egress isolation are independent. Policies are additive unions: a broad allow elsewhere defeats a narrow policy’s intended restriction. Both source egress and destination ingress must permit a connection; permitted replies are implicitly allowed. A CNI/networking implementation supporting NetworkPolicy is mandatory—creating objects alone has no effect. Validate allowed and denied flows. See [NetworkPolicy, lines 45–81 and 105–122](/private/tmp/doktimoi-bench-2-competitor-jeIJrI/docs/concepts/services-networking/network-policies.md:45) and [DNS allowance guidance, lines 215–233](/private/tmp/doktimoi-bench-2-competitor-jeIJrI/docs/concepts/security/multi-tenancy.md:215).

8. **Reject base64 Secrets in Git as protection.** Base64 obscures values but does not keep them secret; repository readers can recover credentials. Remove that storage pattern. Kubernetes Secrets are also unencrypted in etcd by default. Enable encryption at rest, apply least-privilege RBAC, and expose each Secret only to containers that need it. Encryption at rest does not protect a readable Git manifest. Restrict Pod creation and indirect workload creation too: someone authorized to create Pods in a namespace can use that capability to read its Secrets, even without direct Secret-reading permission. See [Secret encoding, lines 282–307](/private/tmp/doktimoi-bench-2-competitor-jeIJrI/docs/concepts/configuration/secret.md:282) and [Secret security prerequisites, lines 35–48](/private/tmp/doktimoi-bench-2-competitor-jeIJrI/docs/concepts/configuration/secret.md:35).

9. **Audit existing PVs individually.** Dynamically provisioned PVs inherit the StorageClass reclaim policy at creation, defaulting to `Delete`. A later class-policy change does not retroactively change existing PV policies; edit or patch those PVs explicitly. After PVC deletion, `Retain` preserves the released PV and data for manual reclamation. Supported `Delete` behavior removes both PV and backing storage. StatefulSet deletion or scale-down is a separate trigger: PVC retention defaults to `Retain`, but configured `whenDeleted` or `whenScaled: Delete` can delete template-created PVCs, subsequently invoking PV reclamation. Verify the documented feature prerequisite before relying on that setting. See [StorageClass, lines 126–135](/private/tmp/doktimoi-bench-2-competitor-jeIJrI/docs/concepts/storage/storage-classes.md:126), [PV reclamation, lines 178–210](/private/tmp/doktimoi-bench-2-competitor-jeIJrI/docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes.md:178), and [StatefulSet retention, lines 391–423](/private/tmp/doktimoi-bench-2-competitor-jeIJrI/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/statefulset.md:391).

10. **Prioritize validation before rollout.** First remove exposed credentials, verify encryption/RBAC, and prove network-policy enforcement. Second audit PV policies and database recovery; for topology-constrained storage, evaluate supported `WaitForFirstConsumer` provisioning. Third establish probe semantics, resource sizing, HPA metrics, minimum replica policy, and surge capacity. Finally stage a rollout, eviction-based drain, node/zone failure, missing-metrics event, and long-request termination while observing readiness and completed requests. Required validation limits include actual startup duration, shutdown/request completion, surviving-zone capacity, CNI enforcement, and database failover/durability. These documents describe mechanisms; they do not establish those application or cluster outcomes. This checklist follows the cited disruption, probe, networking, and HPA constraints; storage scheduling prerequisites appear in [StorageClass, lines 171–199](/private/tmp/doktimoi-bench-2-competitor-jeIJrI/docs/concepts/storage/storage-classes.md:171).
